message.content:
In Christian theology, the focus is generally on the life, teachings, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ as the central narrative of salvation history. Because of this, many Christians regard Jesus as the ultimate fulfillment of prophetic expectation—he is seen as the Messiah prophesied in the Hebrew Scriptures (the Old Testament) and as the divine Son of God in the New Testament.

At the same time, the Old Testament contains numerous prophets whose writings and actions are foundational to Christian faith. Prophets such as Moses (who led Israel out of Egypt and delivered the Law), Isaiah (whose prophecies include messianic expectations), Jeremiah (the “weeping prophet”), and others are highly respected and frequently cited throughout the New Testament. Their messages are viewed as part of the larger narrative that points toward the coming of Christ.

Because Christianity emerged from Judaism, the prophetic tradition is deeply intertwined with its theological development. Different Christian traditions may emphasize certain prophets more than others—for example, some Protestant groups highlight the prophetic role of Paul, while Catholic and Orthodox traditions often stress the continuity between Old Testament prophecy and New Testament revelation.

So, while Jesus is typically regarded as the focal point of Christian belief, the prophets of the Hebrew Bible remain essential figures whose words and deeds shape the broader story of redemption.
